A1.justification: Both PDFs describe COMMA and provide readable text, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. The shared framework, eight retained puzzles, and agent prompts can be reliably matched despite substantial evaluation and presentation changes.

before.justification: V1 reports original AI–AI and AI–human puzzle experiments, performance measurements, and error analyses in Table 1, Figures 2–6, and Appendix C.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark experiments, privacy-leakage measurements, judge-calibration results, and error analyses, with additional performance statistics in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The core Solver–Expert dialogue procedure, screenshot/manual inputs, and action-name execution are retained. Appendix D's general prompts are identical after layout normalization. V2's working-memory and episodic-memory terminology elaborates existing inputs and conversation history rather than establishing a changed agent algorithm.

E1.justification: V1's Button and Dog puzzles are replaced by ATM and Telehealth tasks involving financial privacy and PAD-UFES-20 skin-lesion diagnosis and treatment. Private Information replaces Real-time Reaction as a capability category. Eight other evaluated puzzles are retained, as confirmed by Section 3.3, Table 1, and the appendices.

E2.justification: V2 adds Gemini 2.0, LLaMA 3.2, and LLaVA 1.6 to the reported quantitative comparisons. V1's GPT-4o1 expert comparison, heterogeneous AI pairings, and human-expert pairings disappear. V2's reported human baseline uses a human solver with a GPT-4o expert.

E3.justification: The conversation limit changes from 20 to 10 turns, and v2 explicitly imposes a three-mistake limit. Main evaluation counts increase from 10 to 100 initializations per puzzle for AI pairs and from 3 to 10 for humans. Manual error coding is replaced by a calibrated GPT-4o1 judge, and privacy analysis adds message-level disclosure checks.

E4.justification: V2 adds an ATM privacy-leakage-versus-success analysis and judge calibration, while replacing the manual 50-conversation error study with judge-based analysis and new failure examples. Conversation-length and capability analyses are substantially revised; v1's mistake-versus-turn curves and human-versus-AI capability breakdowns are removed.

E5.justification: V1 reports averages without uncertainty estimates. V2 introduces standard errors throughout its performance tables and capability plots, explicitly attributing variability to puzzle initialization rather than repeated model outputs on identical inputs. Reported sampling increases for AI and human evaluations; the random baseline remains at 100 runs per puzzle.

E6.justification: V1 reports overall partial success rates of 56% for Random, 53% for GPT-4V, and 50% for GPT-4o; v2 reports 18.70%, 27.62%, and 41.74%, respectively. These are replacement results under changed tasks and protocols, not same-setting performance changes. V2 also adds a per-puzzle success-rate table, privacy findings, and 94% judge-calibration accuracy, and replaces error distributions and appendix statistics.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theory, theorems, or proofs. The retained puzzles' mathematical rules, including the LED modulo-26 condition and Color lookup table, are unchanged. The new cognitive-memory framing is conceptual rather than a formal derivation.

C1.justification: V1's headline assertion that AI–AI models, including the GPT series, fail to outperform random is narrowed in v2 to some models; the introduction instead emphasizes human superiority. V2 also makes private-information disclosure a central conclusion and replaces the benchmark's real-time capability emphasis with privacy handling.

C2.justification: V2 replaces interpretations about real-time strengths, human recovery, and model-size surprises with explanations concerning communication failures, role confusion, episodic-memory use, and violations of privacy constraints. It hypothesizes links between these failures and training data. V1's sampling, simulation-to-reality, and deployment limitations are largely retained under Impact Statement.

D1.justification: V2 adds explicit memory/input descriptions, customization information, and ATM/Telehealth rules and data provenance in Appendices A–B. It removes the PyAutoGUI implementation reference and the promise to release benchmark and evaluation code upon acceptance, without replacement access information. General agent prompts, greedy decoding, and hardware disclosure remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands the benchmark's grounding in cognitive science and cognitive agent architecture, including Sumers, Davidson, St Clair-Thompson, and standardized intelligence tests. It also adds recent agent benchmarks, research-agent work, model and dataset sources, and jailbreak literature. These additions extend research positioning beyond routine publication-metadata updates.

P1.justification: Section 3.1 substantially reorganizes the design narrative around agent architecture, intelligence testing, and controllability. Much of Section 5's performance and explanatory prose is rewritten, with corresponding introduction and conclusion revisions. Terminology and author information are edited, and Limitations becomes Impact Statement while retaining most of its content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 is redrawn, Figure 2's cases are rebuilt, error charts are consolidated, and conversation-length and capability plots are redesigned. V2 adds a privacy plot and success-rate table, restructures tables around model rows, and reformats the appendices.

improvement.justification: The larger sampled evaluation, standard-error reporting, direct privacy tests, and narrower random-baseline claim strengthen the paper's evidence and its alignment with its motivation. These gains are tempered by reduced collaboration-pair coverage and unresolved reporting inconsistencies, such as human Maze performance appearing as 70% partial success in Table 1 but 80% success in Table 2. The net quality improvement is therefore limited despite the substantial revision.
